name: Rafael Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Long Acre Farm, nine hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, owned by a farming company and run by a manager called Gill. I'm the general hand, so in November it's carting grain from the store to the lorries, cleaning out the bins, rolling fields after drilling and fixing fences that the deer push over. I start at half seven and I'm home by five unless it's harvest, when nobody's home before midnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to farming fairly late, is that right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did. I was thirty-one years at the paper mill in town, the last twelve as a union shop steward, the person who speaks up for the workers on the floor. The new owners shut it when I was fifty-three, and Gill's dad knew my dad, so here I am. I'm the oldest beginner you'll ever meet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet, and I like that at the end of the day you can see what you did, a clean bin, a rolled field. What wears me out is that I'm still slow. The young lad, Kieran, can back a trailer into the grain store first go, and I'm still doing three shunts with Gill watching from the office window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, it's a fancy search engine. Gill already looks up grain prices on her phone every morning, so maybe she finds them quicker. It doesn't change who sweeps the bins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing for me, I don't use any of it. My phone's six years old and Lena, my partner, does our banking. But I don't trust the companies behind it, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish my forklift ticket, the licence to drive the telehandler in the yard, which Gill's paying for. Keep putting a bit by each month, and get the car through its test in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's like hearing they've made a better calculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you trust the companies, if it doesn't touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen this film. When the mill was sold, the new owners stood in the canteen and said nothing would change, it was just better systems. Two years later the gate was locked and they'd moved the machines to another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did that day at the gate look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was a Friday in February, raining. We'd known for a month, but they still put a padlock on the main gate while we were inside collecting our boxes. I remember a lad called Dariusz holding his hard hat and not knowing whether to keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got around four months of money saved. What's it for, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's for the car dying or Lena's hours being cut at the school kitchen. It's not for anything fun. After the mill, I swore I'd always have enough to get through one bad winter.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's just a fancy search engine and good luck to them. Gill might find grain prices quicker, but it doesn't change who sweeps the bins.
S0.think: I really think it means nothing for me, because I don't use any of it. Still, I don't trust the companies behind it after what happened at the mill.
S0.do: Finishes his forklift ticket, which the farm is paying for. Keeps saving a little each month and gets the car through its test in March.
S0.feel: Calm, as if someone had made a better calculator, with an old distrust underneath.
S0.quote: They still put a padlock on the main gate while we were inside collecting our boxes.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture, Rafael went straight back to the mill closure. His distrust isn't about the technology at all; it's about owners who promise nothing will change. That memory frames every scenario that follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who'll pay for this. Farms already can't find youngsters, and if the office jobs stop taking beginners too, where do they learn anything? I'd say that in the pub and I'd say it at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a beginner myself, at fifty-eight. If companies hire fewer beginners, I might be the last one Long Acre ever takes on. And if I left, I don't think they'd replace me, they'd just buy something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gill for a proper written contract, not the one-page thing I signed. I'd go to the agricultural branch of the union, where I'm the only member from our farm, and ask what they're doing about it. And I'd keep my head down and get better at the trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for Kieran and lads like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Kieran.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's nineteen, on a work placement from the farming college, two days a week. He's quicker than me at everything with a screen, and he's polite to an old man who can't reverse. If the farm stops taking lads like him, the trade dies, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down, but also go to the union. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, and that's how it always was at the mill. You do your job well so nobody can point at you, and then you go to the meeting and make noise. Keeping your head down at work isn't the same as keeping quiet.

S1.say: I'd say the young ones will pay for this, because farms already can't find youngsters. I'd say it in the pub and at the union branch.
S1.think: I think I might be the last beginner Long Acre ever takes on, and nobody would replace me. They'd probably buy a machine instead of hiring.
S1.do: Asks Gill for a proper written contract and goes to the union's agricultural branch to ask what it is doing. Keeps his head down at work and practises reversing the trailer.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the young placement student and others like him.
S1.quote: Keeping your head down at work isn't the same as keeping quiet.
S1.fieldNote: He sees himself as a beginner and an old union man at the same time, and he uses both roles. The worry shifts quickly from himself to Kieran, which is typical of how he talks. When I named the contradiction, he had a clear answer ready, as if he'd lived it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I told you so. First it was the mill, now it's the offices, and they'll do it to every worker if we let them. I'd be at the meeting in the town hall, and I'd tell the politicians arguing on the telly to stop arguing and put rules on these companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not my job I'd lose sleep over, it's my son's. Tomas works in an insurance call centre, sorting claims, and that's exactly the routine office work you're describing. He's thirty-one and saving for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas the spare room is his if he needs it, no questions. I'd stop the extra money going into savings and keep it loose in case he needs help with rent. And I'd go to every union meeting and vote for whoever promises to make these companies pay for what they break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. It's the same anger as the gate, just pointed somewhere new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Tomas, the night he told you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, it isn't you, it's never you. That's what nobody said to me at the mill. Then I'd probably open a beer and we'd watch the football and not talk about it, because that's how we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to choose, your savings or Tomas's deposit, which goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings go first, without thinking. I've got four months and a small mill pension coming. He's got thirty years of work in front of him and nowhere to start.

S2.say: I'd say I told you so, because first it was the mill and now it's the offices. I'd tell the politicians to stop arguing and put rules on these companies.
S2.think: Privately, it's my son Tomas I'd lose sleep over, not my own job. He sorts claims in an insurance call centre, which is exactly that routine office work, and he's saving for a house deposit.
S2.do: Offers Tomas the spare room and stops adding to savings so the money can help with rent. Goes to every union meeting and votes for whoever will make the companies pay.
S2.feel: Angry more than scared, the same anger he felt at the mill gate.
S2.quote: I'd say, son, it isn't you, it's never you. That's what nobody said to me at the mill.
S2.fieldNote: His own job barely came up; his son's did immediately. The line to Tomas was the warmest moment so far, and it came straight out of his own closure. He would spend his small cushion on his son without hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, tax it. If shares and houses are booming while people lose their jobs, then the gains belong to everyone who built the country. I'd march if there was a march, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen in the farm shop queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about the land. If house prices go mad, Long Acre is worth a fortune as building plots or a solar farm. The company doesn't love the soil, it loves the number, and I'm not sure they'd keep growing wheat on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to our member of parliament, a proper letter in pen, because I don't do email. I'd ask Gill straight out whether the company has had offers for the land. And I'd tell Lena we go to the cheaper supermarket from now on, and the money we save goes in the pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My job's safe in this one, they say, but safe on whose land?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said physical jobs are mostly untouched here. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about a year, maybe. A man driving a grain trailer is safe until the field under him gets sold. Nobody needs a robot to get rid of me, a planning permission letter does it fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gill say if you asked her about offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and say, Rafael, I'm only the manager. And that's the truth, she'd find out the same day I did. That's the problem with working for a company, there's nobody in the yard who can actually promise you anything.

S3.say: I'd say tax the gains, because they belong to everyone who built the country. I'd march if there was a march and say it in the farm shop queue.
S3.think: I'd be thinking about the land, because booming prices make Long Acre worth a fortune as building plots or a solar farm. The company loves the number, not the soil.
S3.do: Writes a letter in pen to his member of parliament and asks Gill whether the company has had offers for the land. Switches to a cheaper supermarket and saves the difference.
S3.feel: Anxious, because his job looks safe but the land under it might not be.
S3.quote: Nobody needs a robot to get rid of me, a planning permission letter does it fine.
S3.fieldNote: He found a threat to his physical job that the card didn't mention: the land itself. He has a clear picture of where power sits in a company farm, and it isn't with the manager he works beside. The handwritten letter fits him completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said my whole life: every machine that replaces a worker should pay tax like a worker. The unions need to fight this one properly, not just make statements. I'd stand on the picket line, the protest line outside a workplace, with my bad knee and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm the easiest one on that farm to replace. I'm the slowest, I still leave gaps on the headlands, the turning strips at the field edge, and a robot tractor doesn't. Gill had a self-driving sprayer on a demo last spring and it was better at the corners than me, I watched it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't retrain, I'll be honest, not at sixty with a machine I don't understand. I'd hang on as long as they'd have me, offer to do the jobs nobody's built a robot for yet, cleaning the bins, mending the deer fence. I'd sell the second car, sit down with Lena and work out the earliest I can take my mill pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I watched the gate close on the mill at fifty-three. I'm not going to stand at another gate at sixty and be told a machine does it cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say, that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, we've done this before, Raf, and we were fine. And she'd be right that we were fine, but she didn't see me sitting in the car outside the job centre for forty minutes before I could go in. I don't think I'd tell her that part even now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say Gill offered to train you to watch over the robot tractors. Would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Well, I'd say no, then I'd go home and Lena would talk me round, and I'd say yes. I'd hate every day of learning it and I'd do it anyway, because a job's a job. Don't write down the first answer.

S4.say: Every machine that replaces a worker should pay tax like a worker, and the unions need to fight this one properly. I'd stand on the picket line with my bad knee and all.
S4.think: I'm the easiest one on the farm to replace because I'm the slowest and still leave gaps on the headlands. I watched a self-driving sprayer on a demo do the corners better than me.
S4.do: Hangs on as long as possible, offering to do the jobs no robot does yet, like cleaning bins and mending fences. Sells the second car and works out with Lena the earliest date he can take his mill pension.
S4.feel: Sick at the thought of standing at a second closed gate at sixty; he'd grudgingly take retraining if offered.
S4.quote: Don't write down the first answer.
S4.fieldNote: This is where Rafael's calm broke. He's watched a robot sprayer beat him at his own weak spot, so the threat isn't imagined. The most honest moment was admitting he sat outside the job centre for forty minutes and never told Lena. He refuses retraining and then accepts it in the same breath.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, without a doubt. What would help is a rule that if a farm buys a robot to replace a worker, it pays into a fund for that worker, enough to bridge to the pension. And let men like me take the pension a few years early without losing a third of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Everyone talks about money, but when the mill shut, the money was the easy part. The hard part was the first Monday with nowhere to be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you, Rafael. That's very helpful.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No bother. If you see Gill's company in the papers, you'll know why I was asking.

headlineQuote: I watched the gate close on the mill at fifty-three. I'm not going to stand at another gate at sixty and be told a machine does it cheaper.
portrait: Rafael is a 58-year-old general hand on a company-owned grain and oilseed farm, a former paper mill worker and union shop steward who came to farming after the mill closed. He doesn't use AI and doesn't trust the companies selling it. In the office scenarios he worries for his son, who works in an insurance call centre, and for the land itself if prices soar. With farm robots, he admits he is the easiest worker to replace, refuses retraining, then quietly says he'd take it.
biggestWorry: The last picture, with robots on farms, worries him most, because he is the slowest hand on the farm and has seen a self-driving sprayer beat him.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that farms buying robots pay into a fund to bridge replaced workers to their pension, and the right to take his pension a few years early without a big cut.
